notes.meaning: Passover was the feast that remembered how God rescued Israel from Egypt. The angel of death "passed over" the homes marked with a lamb's blood. The religious leaders wanted a sneaky way to seize Jesus and kill Him. They planned to wait until the feast was over, because the crowds might riot. Yet God's plan overruled theirs. Jesus would die at Passover itself, as the true Passover Lamb.

At a dinner in Bethany, a woman poured very costly, pure perfume over Jesus' head. John's Gospel tells us she was Mary. She broke open the jar. This may mean she broke its seal or its narrow neck. She held nothing back, which reminds us to give Christ our best and our all.

Some guests were angry and called her gift a waste. They said the perfume could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor. John's Gospel shows that Judas spoke first, and others joined in. People who would never give so much themselves often call a generous person wasteful. God does not accept such hasty judgments.
Jesus took her side and told the critics to leave her alone. He called her act a beautiful, good deed. It was good in itself. It came at just the right time. And it was all she could do.

Jesus echoes Deuteronomy 15:11, which says the poor will always be among God's people. His words are a gentle hint that He would soon leave them. Caring for the poor is good. Still, it does not excuse us from showing special love to Jesus Himself. Some commentators add that Christ now wants to be honored every day by our care for the poor.

Jesus gave her act an even deeper meaning than she may have planned. He said she had prepared His body for burial ahead of time. When the women later came with spices to anoint His body, He had already risen. So this was her chance. Her gift pointed to His coming death.

Jesus promised that her story would be told wherever the good news is preached. Only He could promise a memory that lasts as long as the gospel. Those who honor Christ, He will honor. Her deed still fills the world with its fragrance.

Judas, one of Jesus' own twelve closest followers, went to the leaders to hand Him over. Love of money was his great weakness, and the devil tempted him right there. Luke says Satan entered him. The leaders were delighted and promised to pay him. Matthew tells us the price was thirty pieces of silver. Judas then looked for a quiet moment, away from the crowds. Sin is a downhill road: once people start, they keep going.

This was the day the Passover lamb was killed for the meal. The disciples asked where they should prepare it. By keeping the Passover as the law required, Jesus placed Himself under the law for our sake. He ate it at the usual time, just as other Jews did.

Jesus sent two disciples, Peter and John, with very exact directions. A man carrying a water jar would lead them to a house with a large upstairs room. The room would be spread with carpets and couches, ready for the meal. Only Jesus' perfect knowledge could foresee such small details. Some think He used this sign to keep the place hidden from Judas.
The disciples found everything just as Jesus had said. They got the Passover meal ready, including the lamb and the foods eaten with it. Jesus' word proved true down to the smallest detail.
That evening Jesus came with the Twelve to eat the Passover. Judas was there too. Jesus knew what Judas planned, but He did not shut him out, because his sin was not yet known to others.

As they lay around the table eating, Jesus said one of them would betray Him. To betray someone you share a meal with was a deep wrong. Jesus may have said this to stir Judas's conscience while there was still time to turn back.

The disciples were grieved, and one by one they asked, "Surely not I?" They suspected themselves more than each other. They trusted Jesus' words more than their own hearts. That is a good example for us.

Jesus said the betrayer was one who dipped into the same dish with Him. Sharing a dish was a sign of close friendship. That made the betrayal even worse. The others did not seem to grasp who He meant.

Jesus would die just as God had planned and the Old Testament had foretold. Yet God's plan did not force Judas to sin, and it does not excuse him. God can bring good out of people's sins, but they are still guilty. So Jesus warned that it would be better for that man if he had never been born.

Here Jesus began the Lord's Supper, also called Communion. He blessed the bread, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, "This is My body." The broken bread pictures His body broken for us. It is food for the soul, so only a little bread is needed as a sign. He meant it to continue until He comes again.

Jesus took the cup, thanked God, and they all drank from it. The cup held "the fruit of the vine," probably wine mixed with water. Taking and drinking reminds us to receive Christ's death for ourselves, as food and drink for our souls.

Jesus called the cup His "blood of the covenant." A covenant is a binding promise, and here it is the new covenant of grace. His blood is the price that buys our freedom from sin, so that God is at peace with us. The old pictures in the Passover now give way to the real thing. His blood was poured out "for many," so each repenting sinner can ask, "If for many, why not for me?"

differ.view: The cup is a lasting sign and memorial of Christ's blood, shed to set up the new covenant. All who believe in Him may receive its gracious promises.
